newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwait parliament approves $14 bln 1996/97 budget.
newsitem.headline: Kuwait parliament approves $14 bln 1996/97 budget.

text.p: Kuwait's oppositon-dominated parliament on Tuesday retroactively approved a 4.21 billion dinar ($14 billion) state budget with a forecast net deficit of 1.21 billion dinars for the fiscal year which started July 1.
Although the budget was passed unanimously by 37 deputies present after a three-hour debate some MPs criticised the government's policy to finance the deficit.
Total revenue in the 1996/97 budget was put at three billion dinars, including 2.56 billion dinars in oil earnings.
By law 10 percent of total revenues is placed in a fund for future generations, making the gross projected deficits 1.51 billion dinars for 1996/97 and 1.61 billion dinars for 1995/96.
Deficits are traditionally financed from general reserves in the form of a debt to the future generations fund.
"This is a situation which is totally unacceptable," opposition veteran MP Ahmad al-Khatib told parliament.
Kuwait, like some other fellow Gulf Arab states, plans to balance the budget by 2000. They blame huge 1991 Gulf War costs and previous weak world oil prices for their deficits.

"The future...is in jeopardy because of this mentality," added Khatib who is not seeking re-election in the October 7 polls. "I hope the next assembly...would lay the necessary rules for the new shift and refuse any de-facto situations".
Finance Minister Nasser al-Rodhan told MPs "growth in the deficit has been stopped".
The budget passed by parliament forecast a 1995/96 deficit of 1.32 billion dinars and revenues of 2.91 billion dinars.
Liberal MP Ahmad al-Rubai, who resigned in September as education minister to seek re-election, proposed to parliament the introduction of income tax.
"There is no solution for the current deficit without a tax regime...If we get you the finance minister of Japan not Rodhan he will not be able to solve the situation for you."
In July the government said it expected to halve the 1995/96 forecast deficit mainly due to higher world oil prices.
Oil revenue is the budget was calculated at a conservative weighted average price of $13 a barrel, unchanged from the past two years although world prices have been much higher this year.
About half of the oil revenue and more than a third of total income is spent on salaries of 1.25 billion dinars in the wellfare state of 700,000 Kuwaiti citizens.
"You are employing unproductive citizens," Rubai complained.
The government has repeatedly said it would not cut salaries of Kuwaitis in its efforts to balance the budget.

The Defence Ministry was allocated 460 million dinars but the funds do not include Kuwait's arms procurement programme worth $12 billion in the 1992-2004 period as part of efforts to rebuild the military after the 1990 Iraqi invasion.
Since the Gulf crisis, Kuwait's foreign investment portfolio has fallen to about $35 billion from over $100 billion. Revenue from the portfolio is not included in the budget. ($1=0.3 dinars)
